RR Auction has concluded the auction for Steve Jobs' 1968 science fair project, with the handmade exhibit ultimately selling for $34,375. Below are the details.

"Overall condition is very good to excellent"

A few days ago, we reported on the auction of a science fair project created by Steve Jobs in 1968 during his second year of junior high school.

At the time, bidding for the project—focused on silicon-controlled rectifiers and featuring two demonstration circuits along with a 10-page report—had not yet reached $3,000 in the online auction.

As one of the items in the "Steve Jobs and the Computer Revolution: The 50th Anniversary of Apple Auction (Part Two)," bidding for this piece has now concluded, and as reported by MacRumors, the final sale price reached $34,375.

According to RR Auction, the project "was preserved for decades at the famous 'Apple garage' property," kept by Jobs' family the entire time. His stepbrother John Chovanec said that Jobs repeatedly refused to take the project back, and so it eventually ended up with Chovanec.

The "Steve Jobs and the Computer Revolution: The 50th Anniversary of Apple Auction (Part Two)" presented nearly 150 rare Apple and technology-related collectibles, including a business card signed by Steve Jobs, a batch of electronic components privately owned by Jobs, and a 1983 letter in which he declined a speaking invitation. These sold for $156,658, $27,188, and $24,695 respectively.

However, the highest-priced lot in this auction was a working Apple-1 computer, one of the 50 units from the second production batch, which ultimately sold for $499,363.

Do you collect any rare Apple memorabilia? Feel free to share in the comments section.
